item.title: How do you write lyrics or dialogue good without sounding pretentious? I feel like an obvious answer might be "well that's what you think. who cares what people think." ME! I care what people think! If I put a thing out into the world and everyone thinks it's kinda cringe and pretentious then I will feel bad! Do you also feel these things? I guess it really depends on what you actually want, I guess. If you wanna sell your art as a product then different things matter than if you want to just get validation for it or if you just want to create something for your own sake. Sigh. I dunno if I'm answering all my own questions here I don't know. what do you think
item.description:
3.2.26 12:32 am
Q: How do you write lyrics or dialogue good without sounding pretentious? I feel like an obvious answer might be "well that's what you think. who cares what people think." ME! I care what people think! If I put a thing out into the world and everyone thinks it's kinda cringe and pretentious then I will feel bad! Do you also feel these things? I guess it really depends on what you actually want, I guess. If you wanna sell your art as a product then different things matter than if you want to just get validation for it or if you just want to create something for your own sake. Sigh. I dunno if I'm answering all my own questions here I don't know. what do you think
A: suppose you deeply care what other people will think, and there's no reason why you wouldn't, in fact the only recipe you have for judging that is what you yourself think, and feel. in fact, most (all) of the most cringe content is a direct result of this guessing game, everyone guessing what someone else is going to like. but getting back to the first thing you asked, i never found out if you do or dont think your own work is pretentious. your question seems to stop just shy of revealing this important detail for me

item.title: can instrumental become the lyrics once you run out of things to say with language?
item.description:
3.2.26 1:37 am
Q: can instrumental become the lyrics once you run out of things to say with language?
A: sure. in fact, a standard and powerful maneuver, across all kinds of music, is this: sing some words, play a riff. sing some words, play a riff. Or the other way around, play a riff, sing some words. etc. The words will explain what the riff is about, and the riff will demonstrate how to feel about what the words said

item.title: Why do you think our brains enjoy the harmonic intervals that we do? A perfect fifth sounds so nice it's almost nothing, but a 2nd interval sounds discordant and tense. It seems like our brains enjoy frequencies that nest inside each other neatly. Do you think it's some fundamental mathematical principle of our universe that any neural network that forms out of the matter inside it will gravitate towards neatly nesting frequency combos like fifths and octaves, while sensing other closer intervals as more chaotic sounding? Or do you think to some other species, a 2nd or 9th could sound perfectly resolved while a fifth sounds discordant? I ate the weed oil out of my weed pen and now I think I'm stuck on one of those "do we all see colors differently" types of unanswerable questions. I'd love to read your thoughts though.
item.description:
3.4.26 6:31 am
Q: Why do you think our brains enjoy the harmonic intervals that we do? A perfect fifth sounds so nice it's almost nothing, but a 2nd interval sounds discordant and tense. It seems like our brains enjoy frequencies that nest inside each other neatly. Do you think it's some fundamental mathematical principle of our universe that any neural network that forms out of the matter inside it will gravitate towards neatly nesting frequency combos like fifths and octaves, while sensing other closer intervals as more chaotic sounding? Or do you think to some other species, a 2nd or 9th could sound perfectly resolved while a fifth sounds discordant? I ate the weed oil out of my weed pen and now I think I'm stuck on one of those "do we all see colors differently" types of unanswerable questions. I'd love to read your thoughts though.
A: here's what seems to be happening: in abscence of any tangible definition of what's good or not good or what anything exactly means, it becomes an irresistible miracle when someone still manages to communicate nonetheless. Like a pile of paperclips. there is no definition for the rules of communicating with paperclips, but then you watch an artist come along and boom they communicate something to you with paperclips. like 'how did they do that', and it may feel like a total miracle, which it is, but in the broader picture it's not surprising that this works. it's just impossible to explain

item.description:
3.4.26 10:09 pm
Q: I'm writing up a concept for a video game and its surrounding world/story/etc from my head onto a big text document. Do you think describing its music in terms of a genre + country + decade (i.e. "90s Japanese soul" or "2000s sambass") is a good thing to do, or should I focus on describing the particular sounds/instruments/feelings when I imagine the game's songs instead? The game's world won't contain our countries, decades or any human history or humans at all, so I don't want to describe it in a way that makes any eventual musicians overly worry about anachronisms and real-world counterparts. Or is describing music in text the wrong way to go overall? Also, are you aware of any goth-subculture music with flutes and/or very prominent bass? One of my planned characters would probably play this music/these instruments as a hobby, and I'm not sure if it exists yet
A: do anything you can to describe something. ideally the only way to describe something is by showing them the actual thing. but it sounds like you are looking to collaborate, so you'll need to communicate with them about what you think youre going for. grab onto anything you can. when collaborative professionals communicate to each other about what they're thinking about for their movie, on their song, whatever they're working on, they're surely constantly referencing things that already exist, while also making it clear that none of these could be a perfect description because youre attempting something to describe something that doesnt exist yet. so it's usually a combination of multiple different references. like this element from this movie, combined with that element from that book, etc etc. or like "what if this character from this movie was in this other situation instead". or "its like this but without the that" etc etc. these are the kind of conversations that you'll hear among professional creative collaborators, almost ubiquitously, across the board

item.title: I've got two questions for the price of one (but I marked it up 200% right before asking, art of the deal baby) 1. When you write chord progressions, do you think of them as overlapping individual melodies that should stay cohesive, or do you just hear each chord as it's own thing? Like in a C Amin G F progression, you can think of t first E as starting a melody that goes e-c-b-a, or the first G note going g-e-d-c. Do you hear these individual melodies and try to keep them coherent, or do you just feel the texture of the chord? 2. Can a melody or chord progression function the same way in any key? I don't have perfect pitch, so I tend to just hear the intervals between notes, and a fifth feels the same to me whether it's A and E or G and D. The context around the intervals tends to be what makes them sound a certain way. I tend to choose a key based on where my voicings are at to avoid things sounding muddy, but if I shift my entire song one semitone down it doesn't usually make a difference to me (unless I listened to it one semitone up first and it's fresh in my mind).

Like in a C Amin G F progression, you can think of t first E as starting a melody that goes e-c-b-a, or the first G note going g-e-d-c. Do you hear these individual melodies and try to keep them coherent, or do you just feel the texture of the chord? 2. Can a melody or chord progression function the same way in any key? I don't have perfect pitch, so I tend to just hear the intervals between notes, and a fifth feels the same to me whether it's A and E or G and D. The context around the intervals tends to be what makes them sound a certain way. I tend to choose a key based on where my voicings are at to avoid things sounding muddy, but if I shift my entire song one semitone down it doesn't usually make a difference to me (unless I listened to it one semitone up first and it's fresh in my mind).
A: I've got two questions for the price of one (but I marked it up 200% right before asking, art of the deal baby) 1. When you write chord progressions, do you think of them as overlapping individual melodies that should stay cohesive, or do you just hear each chord as it's own thing? "when you write a sentence, do you think of it like overlapping individual words that should stay cohesive, or do you just hear each word as its own thing?" the reason i ask you this is because you must be familiar with sentnces, both written and spoken. so you must have some experience in this. and i promise you the answer for music is qualitatively the same Like in a C Amin G F progression, you can think of t first E as starting a melody that goes e-c-b-a, or the first G note going g-e-d-c. Do you hear these individual melodies and try to keep them coherent, or do you just feel the texture of the chord? i know ive beaten this analogy like a dead horse, but i'm dreadfully serious with it. "do you hear individual letters in a word and try to keep them coherent, or do you just feel the texture of the letter" hopefully by now youre thinking something like "i have no idea how the words come to me, i just speak. and im usually thinking about what im saying, not about the words and certainly much less the letters" 2. Can a melody or chord progression function the same way in any key? I don't have perfect pitch, so I tend to just hear the intervals between notes, and a fifth feels the same to me whether it's A and E or G and D. yes, this is good. this is normal. this means you are hearing music like music. some children become cursed when they learn to memorize all the notes cold. then they're stuck hearing music non-musically. they dont even hear chords and melodies, they just hear individual notes, and they often cant even hear multiple ones at a time. where as with 'musical' hearing such as you have, you'll be able to instantly recognize pretty much anything a reasonable song can throw at you, in most circumstances The context around the intervals tends to be what makes them sound a certain way. I tend to choose a key based on where my voicings are at to avoid things sounding muddy, but if I shift my entire song one semitone down it doesn't usually make a difference to me (unless I listened to it one semitone up first and it's fresh in my mind). it sounds like youve got the hang of this. the bad news is now youre cursed with knowing how much of a weird and misunderstood question "do you have perfect pitch" is

item.title: When you're an artist, nothing is off-limits. Video gamemaking, board gamemaking, conlangs, worldbuilding, etc., everything that we're supposed to look down on as "not real art" is fair game for sandbox exploration just as much as "real art" (e.g. songwriting, embroidery, cinematography, and so on). Am I on to something?
item.description:
3.16.26 2:03 am
Q: When you're an artist, nothing is off-limits. Video gamemaking, board gamemaking, conlangs, worldbuilding, etc., everything that we're supposed to look down on as "not real art" is fair game for sandbox exploration just as much as "real art" (e.g. songwriting, embroidery, cinematography, and so on). Am I on to something?
A: sure except i dont think the public opinion of the definition of 'real art' is even as well defined as you think it is. For example, if you had listed all 7 of those things in the same set, and asked me which ones do i think are 'supposed' to be considered 'real art', i wouldnt necessarily sort them out in the same ways you did. in general it's common for people to be slow in accepting newer forms of art. so generally when people say something is 'not real art', they are usually talking about something newer than whatever else they have in mind as 'real art'. in fact, just the other day i was listening to a film director from yesteryear talking about how films back then were not very well respected as art, until television came along, and then the filmmakers were very excited because now they have 'something to look down on'. this cat and mouse chase continues on through the ages, and it can be quite amusing to follow

item.title: what's the best way to write a brigde in a song? and what's its purpose?
item.description:
3.16.26 8:56 pm
Q: what's the best way to write a brigde in a song? and what's its purpose?
A: defining what the heck a bridge is is a lot like trying to hold a pile of sand in your hand. If you are in a position where you think you are 'supposed' to make a 'bridge', you will have 2 problems. 1: 'bridge' will be undefinable, and 2: you wont have any feeling that you need it. Another way to say this: it's a lot like when youve been sitting in a chair for a certin amount of time and you just need to stretch. and you say, "what's the best way to stretch, and what's it's purpose"..... no idea. no need to worry about or think about it. if you feel like stretching, you'll stretch and you'll automatically know how. To re-iterate what i'm trying to say another way: the worst thing you can do for a 'bridge' is to think it is 1 official thing that is supposed to happen. the only thing that really defines it is that it's something different, something unexpected. so if you try to pin down what it's supposed to be, that's a one-way ticket to bridge-failure, which usually occurs when people try to put a bridge because they think theyre supposed to, when it actually doesnt feel right. Maybe a broader way to look at this problem is, "what do you do after 2 full rounds of the main form of the song". and the answer is drastically different in every song, and often you dont even need to do anything. in general the most common problem is to be out of touch with what it actually feels like to have heard the song all the way up to this point

Is the time you have spent away been filled with stretches of time without knowing what to do or has it been spent mostly trying to figure out how to develop existing ideas? someone about 5 questions down has a similar problem to me. the overload of ideas literally clogs the system. every day of my life for at least the past 20 years i've been living under the looming threat that it may be completely impossible to unclog the system. it's a miracle i've ever gotten anything through Also, I would suspect that with the amount of time that has passed one would eventually get tired with the idea that made you realize that your absence would be a prolonged one because of how long it would have taken and how the mind naturally wonders into new things. Was there a moment that made you realize that it was going to be a while or have you forgotten? around april 2023 i decided to try a new selection strategy that i've always wanted to try, because i just couldnt take the terminal fear and anxiety i've always had with the selection process. the strategy was to select as many things as i want. i ended up choosing 10 (i was actually surprised that i didnt choose more). So it was pretty obvious that that would take a hideously long time, and the truth is i was obviously running from something. so deep down on some level i probably knew that i was living in a fantasy world. and i've been running from the consequences all this time. just facing up to them now, and despite how scary it is i'm starting to get the warm eager feelings i got in feb 2014, or aug 2018, or feb 2022, etc. Which was fully predictable also. The solutions this time wont be quite the same as last time, because there were reasons why the past solutions eventually failed and were untenable, but i'm very excited nonetheless, mostly because i'm ultimately pretty confident in my ability to solve problems. And in fact, the 'clog' phenomenon actually builds up a monsterously strong desire to explode. You'd think this wouldn't still be effective after the fact that i've already gotten a lot of stuff out over the years, but in fact it feels stronger each time. there is the vividly unshakable feeling that the majority of my best work has yet to come out

item.title: I had an idea for a novel recently about someone who thinks they have died and feels like instead of moving into a space after death, they've gone out the other side into a space before birth, which are one and the same. item.title: I've got no experience making music. Spent a few decades wishing I knew how to, but kind of assuming I'd missed my window to learn, and that me not knowing all the formal language around compositon was an insurmountable barrier. Thank you for contributing to me unlearning that! I'm giving it a try now. Since I have no instruments and no money, I'm starting with a sequencer. It's a sequencer with deliberately limited options, which has been helping me to not get overwhelmed. I have enough understanding of notes and octaves just from cultural osmosis that I'm able to kind of guess at what combination of notes will make the sounds I want, and feel out a couple adjustments with trial and error. It's felt good so far! But I'm hitting a wall now. I'm struggling to connect any of what I create the way I see it connecting in my head. Individual parts ("phrases," I think?) come out the way I envision them, but something's getting lost in translation in the space between them. Massaging out mistranslations in the individual parts is trial and error, but how do I feel out the connective tissue? It feels much more abstract. My gut instinct was that it's similar to how you weave a thread between sentences in English to connect them, but something's missing in that approach. I'm also finding I have absolutely no natural sense for writing rhythm instruments at all, and suspect that's playing a big part. As though I'm envisioning a rhythm I can't clearly hear, and thus never comes out right. It's just this formless energy humming in the background, but I feel certain there's something tangible within that. How do you learn to give form to rhythm?

item.title: by the time I get home, even after feeling rested, I cant seem to work on anything at all. do you have any advice for this?
item.description:
3.23.26 9:40 pm
Q: by the time I get home, even after feeling rested, I cant seem to work on anything at all. do you have any advice for this?
A: here's what i would do, but i have no idea if it will work for you. do a brainstorm, either in text or in audio, and just think out loud about what you wish you could do, without any pressure to do it today. this might be more enjoyable at first than actually working on something. in the course of a brainstorm, you may get some clarity about exactly what steps you might want to take, then you can schedule an exact time for tomorrow (preferably the same time as when youre brainstorming, but 24 hours later) to do a very specific step. then after doing it (the next day), brainstorm a little more to evaluate where you are, and make the next plan for the next day. mountains are moved this way

item.title: since when do you know that you need to do things to get better at them? i'm asking because this seemingly obvious fact took me very long to realize, partly due to numerous textbooks, pieces of documentation, and educational materials that reinforce the unconscious belief that you know how to do things once you've read an explanation about it. I wonder if it'd be good for these materials to state things more explicitely, or if it's obvious to most people and i'm looking for a scapegoat to avoid taking responsibility for my general incompetence
item.description:
3.29.26 8:41 am
Q: since when do you know that you need to do things to get better at them? i'm asking because this seemingly obvious fact took me very long to realize, partly due to numerous textbooks, pieces of documentation, and educational materials that reinforce the unconscious belief that you know how to do things once you've read an explanation about it. I wonder if it'd be good for these materials to state things more explicitely, or if it's obvious to most people and i'm looking for a scapegoat to avoid taking responsibility for my general incompetence
A: i dont know where the idea comes from that an instruction is sufficient for being able to actually do something. i think it probably comes from a general overestimation for how accurate language is. i really started realizing this actually when i started learning foreign languages. and then all these memories come flooding back to me from early childhood as i remember learning english for the first time. and then also it becomes impossible to avoid the analogy to 'walking.' thats why i always go around saying 'did you learn to walk by being told how'.... and also reminding people 'and by the way how long did it take'

item.description:
3.29.26 5:35 pm
Q: I was driving earlier and saw a road sign that said SLOW. At first I was like, ok, maybe they just didnt want to put in a different speed limit sign for a new, lower speed limit. But they already put in the SLOW sign, so it wasnt just a matter of not wanting to put up a different speed limit sign. How fast is SLOW? It was on a road with a 30mph speed limit... so like 5mph? 10? 15? And then there was no second sign to say "YOU CAN GO FASTER NOW", so how far am I supposed to drive slower than the speed limit?
A: the SLOW sign is a suggestion, not a law. the SPEED LIMIT sign is a law. Sometimes you see things that contradict each other. For example, you might see School Zone 20mph, and then right next to it "Low Speed Vehicles Prohibited". i happen to know the second sign means no tractors, but the two signs were probably not designed with the intention of co-existing near each other. Signage, like pinecones, are not perfect

item.title: bro i had a disappointing ass dinner. the server kept hyping us up abt how the food uses so many spices therefore it's super flavorful. Tell me WHERE were the spices when i got my entree because that shit was BLAND AS FUCK & the whole appeal of the restaurant was that it's supposed to be flavorful moroccan cuisine. is the flavor in the room with us because it must still be in morocco. have you had a similar experience recently?? What would you do in this situation??
item.description:
4.2.26 2:25 am
Q: bro i had a disappointing ass dinner. the server kept hyping us up abt how the food uses so many spices therefore it's super flavorful. Tell me WHERE were the spices when i got my entree because that shit was BLAND AS FUCK & the whole appeal of the restaurant was that it's supposed to be flavorful moroccan cuisine. is the flavor in the room with us because it must still be in morocco. have you had a similar experience recently?? What would you do in this situation??
A: there is something particularly humorous about something being hyped way up and then actually being the opposite of what it's hyped to be. this reminds me many many years ago at burger thing, when they first introduced the "chicken fries" (or maybe one of the many times the re-introduced them), they come in a tall, top-heavy box. the box is somehow designed so it has a sauce holder on top. a little slot where you can put the sauce container. They had arrows pointing to it and then had a description "Sauce goes here. Yup, we promoted the guy who invented it." whether or not they actually promoted someone, i dont know or care, but here's the thing: the sauce fits fine in the slot, but as soon as you start taking the fries out, to eat them, the box immediately falls over. it only works when the box is full of chicken fries. this brilliant invention immediately fails as soon as you start using it. What would have seemed mildly silly, became an even more humorous spectacle based on the hype story written on the box. i'm also thinking of debut of the tesla cybertruck, where they demonstrated the unbreakable windows by hitting it with a sledge hammer and the window immediately broke "what you do in this situation" is you collect stories like this for amusement

A: i mean it's like whether you put the cow on the right side of the barn or the left, in your farm picture. but i think in time you will stop calling them 'inversions' because there is really no 'default' order. actually they way they're most often used in music, chances are, will be in a different order from the 'default' order you may have learned. the truth is, if the page says "C", that doesnt say it all. either the writer or arranger or just you the player with good judgement, will have to decide which octaves to play those notes in. item.title: Recently I realized that I had forgotten some lessons that I learned many years ago, and that I needed to teach myself those same lessons again. A: you can get into this game of organizing all your wisdom and everything you know, but ultimately youre not going to prevent the ebb and flow of different realizations, different mentalities, different strategies, etc. It's nice to write things down and compare notes, but you can't promise yourself to uphold every mindset all the time
